title: Global bond sell-off pushes 10-year Treasury yield to highest since 2002
content:
Emily Herbert and Ian Smith in London, William Sandlund in Hong Kong and Leo Lewis in Tokyo

Published October 1 2026

Updated October 1 2026

Could you be the FT’s top trader?

A global bond rout briefly pushed US Treasury yields to their highest level since 2002 on Thursday while Eurozone borrowing costs surged, as pressure from the Iran war energy shock on public finances intensified around the world.

Yields on 10-year Treasuries climbed as much as 0.05 percentage points to 5.34 per cent, a level last seen almost a quarter of a century ago, as traders warned the $32tn US government bond market, an anchor for global finance, was caught in a “vicious loop” of selling. They later rallied to 5.24 per cent, down 0.05 percentage points on the day.

Meanwhile, UK 30-year gilt yields climbed above 6 per cent for the first time since 1998 but later eased to 5.93 per cent.

Traders had been “dazzled” by the scale of the recent government bond sell-off, said Rob Subbaraman, head of global macro research at Nomura, adding that this was driven by higher inflation and concerns about the sustainability of government deficits.

The surge in yields has swept across the global economy , raising borrowing costs for consumers, businesses and governments. US conventional 30-year mortgage rates jumped 0.25 percentage points — the biggest increase in four years — to 7.28 per cent this week, according to Freddie Mac data released on Thursday.

Investors have warned that jumps in yields in recent trading sessions have been exacerbated by hedge funds and other big investors, which have been forced to ditch long-term debt to counteract the effect of rising rates on their broader debt portfolios, or to unwind lossmaking trades as the market has sold off.

Brent crude, the international oil benchmark, was up 3.2 per cent to $101.15 a barrel on Thursday, adding upward pressure to yields.

Mike Bell, head of market strategy at RBC BlueBay Asset Management, said: “You’ve got to a position where lots of people are getting stopped out of long positions or thinking: I don’t want to hold this as [the yield] keeps going up.”

On a choppy day for Eurozone bond markets, France’s 10-year yield rose as much as 0.1 percentage points to 4.96 per cent on Thursday, touching its highest level since mid-2002 in intraday trading.

The swings came as the French government put forward a 2027 budget with €43bn of cuts and tax increases amid rising worries over the health of its public finances.

The euro dropped as much as 1 per cent to a 16-month low of $1.1216, buffeted by higher oil prices and what analysts said were rising risks from the bond market sell-off. European bank shares fell, with BNP Paribas down 3.6 per cent and Deutsche Bank falling 2.6 per cent.

Italy’s 10-year government bond yield was up 0.05 percentage points to 4.69 per cent, taking its spread with German debt to 1 percentage point for the first time since March.

Italy and other Eurozone government bonds were starting to suffer from “spillovers” from the French bond sell-off, said Pooja Kumra, rates strategist at TD Securities. “[The] moves have been significant and will need some vocal intervention from policymakers.”

European stocks fell as investors fretted over possible fallout from higher yields. The region-wide Stoxx Europe 600 stock index dipped 1.3 per cent while the FTSE 100 fell 1.7 per cent.

In the US, the S&P 500 and Nasdaq 100 were about flat just after midday. Wall Street stocks have been relatively resilient to the sell-off in debt, buoyed by investors’ bullishness about the AI theme.

Harriet Ballard, a portfolio manager at Aviva Investors, said she remained positive on the equity market, despite the pressure from higher interest rates, because “AI-linked sectors have been better insulated by strong earnings”.

Lifted by rising yields, the dollar was up 0.5 per cent against a basket of its peers to its highest level since April last year.

Bond markets have for months been racked by fears over the spectre of higher inflation triggered by the Iran war’s energy shock, which has pushed the relationship between oil prices and Treasury yields to its tightest point since 1990 . This has been intensified by robust US economic data, which has further fed expectations of higher interest rates.

Traders are braced for further swings, with the Ice BofA Move index of implied volatility in Treasuries approaching the high reached in the first weeks of the conflict.

As the bond worries spread through Asian markets earlier, Japanese 10-year bond yields rose 0.04 percentage points to 3.1 per cent, close to a multi-decade high.

Mitul Kotecha, head of Asian foreign exchange and emerging markets macro strategy at Barclays, said the pressure on Japanese bonds was down to “a combination of the contagion of what’s happening in the US market and, to some extent, uncertainty about [the Bank of Japan] tightening [rates]”.

“It’s the fiscal concerns that continue to play in the market,” he added.

Corporate credit spreads have also widened in recent days as investors worry that the volatility in government bond markets could spread into the credit markets that determine companies’ borrowing costs.

The additional interest rate paid by European investment-grade companies over government bond yields has ticked higher to almost 0.9 percentage points this week, the highest level since April, according to ICE BofA data.

“There is a risk that credit spreads follow [yields higher],” said Andrew Jackson, head of investment at Vontobel Asset Management.

Inflation data in several European countries — including Germany, France and Italy — on Wednesday showed higher price pressures than analysts had expected, adding to investors’ fears that the energy price shock is feeding through into economic strain, although US data showed a drop in the Federal Reserve’s preferred inflation measure.

Investors have been struck by a relentless march higher in global bond yields where problems in each market, including Japan, France and the US, are feeding off each other.

“As [yields] move up, they are pulling each other up,” said Guy Miller, chief market strategist at Zurich.

title: UK-Iranian dual national arrested over RAF Fairford incident, police say
content:
A UK-Iranian dual national has been arrested on suspicion of preparation of terrorist acts in connection with the incident at RAF Fairford, counter-terror police have said.

The 25-year-old man was arrested in Westminster, London. Two properties in the area have been searched.

Five men in their twenties who were arrested near the Gloucestershire airbase on Sunday remain on police bail. All five were UK nationals from London.

Counter-terror police are considering "all possible angles - including foreign state involvement", the force's senior national coordinator Vicki Evans said.

"The investigation into circumstances surrounding events in Gloucestershire is hugely complex, and our specialist teams are interrogating multiple lines of enquiry," she said.

"I'd like to thank the public for their continued support and patience whilst we work through this investigation."

Police had initially given the dual UK-Iranian national's age as 27 and said a second man had been questioned under caution, but in a later update said that this was not the case.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said on Wednesday there were "strong indications" that Iran played a part in the incident. He did not provide further details, and Tehran has strongly denied any involvement.

The five men were arrested in the early hours of Sunday morning after "three suspicious vehicles" were reported travelling towards the base operated by the US Air Force (USAF), sparking a major security incident.

The BBC understands that one of the men had dialled 999 himself, about an hour before a local farmer alerted police to a "large group" of masked men near the vehicles.

They were arrested on suspicion of explosives offences and later on suspicion of preparing a terrorist act, before being released on bail on Monday in what police called an "investigative decision" that was "grounded in experience and strategy".

Police said a quantity of petrol but no explosive devices were found during searches of vans near the site.

The group were aged between 23 and 25. Four live in Westminster and one in Camden, and searches of their homes were carried out.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Monday that "the hands of a foreign actor" had clearly been involved in the incident at the base, which has been used as a forward operating location by the USAF for decades.

In recent months, US bombers have taken off from the airbase for the Middle East, after the UK approved a US request to use it for what it called defensive strikes on Iran.

On Thursday, the British ambassador to Iran met the country's foreign ministry at the request of the Iranian government.

title: Renee Good: Family of US woman killed by ICE agent sues Trump officials
content:
The family of a woman who was killed by an immigration agent in Minneapolis has announced two lawsuits against the US government and members of the Trump administration.

Renee Good, a US citizen, was shot to death by an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer during a major immigration sweep in January. Millions watched the video recorded of her killing and residents of the Minnesota city took to the streets to protest.

One lawsuit blames the government for her death, claiming the operation created "an unprecedented environment for state-sponsored violence", a lawyer for the family said.

A White House spokeswoman in a statement called the lawsuits "baseless".

The lawsuits were brought by Good's brother, Brent Ganger, and her partner, Becca Good.

Speaking publicly for the first time since the shooting, Becca Good told a news conference on the lawsuits on Thursday: "The whole world had to watch as our entire universe was destroyed."

"We were all robbed," she said as she described how the shooting affected their three children.

In one of the lawsuits, the family accuses the government of "battery, assault, false imprisonment, intentional infliction of emotional distress and negligence that caused Renee's death", according to the family's lawyer.

It cites the Federal Tort Claims Act, which allows citizens to sue the government for personal injury, death or property damage caused by the negligence of federal employees.

The second lawsuit targets ICE officer Jonathan Ross, who shot Good, as well as White House Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller, former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem, White House border tsar Tom Homan and others, alleging a "conspiracy to interfere with civil rights by senior federal officials, federal immigration enforcement agents and private actors".

"Our government has become a grave and mortal threat to its own citizens," the family's lawyer, Antonio Romanucci told Thursday's news conference.

In her statement, Lauren Bis, a spokeswoman for the White House, said the deaths of Americans at the hands of illegal immigrants should merit "equal coverage" by news media.

She also said the government will "vigorously defend these baseless civil lawsuits".

Trump had initially blamed Good's own actions for her death, saying just hours after she was killed that she "violently, wilfully and viciously ran over the ICE officer". Weeks later, he called her death a "tragedy" and said agents were sometimes "going to make a mistake".

The White House also shared a comment from Trump where he said: "I would bet you that she, under normal circumstances, was a very solid, wonderful person - but her actions were pretty tough."

He also said ICE agents' work "is being made very difficult" and that "when you look at the way that car was pulled away… there are a couple versions of that tape that are very very bad," according to the comments.

Good was a 37-year-old mother of three who had just moved to the city. She was shot on 7 January in a traffic stop, which immigration authorities said occurred after she made "an attempt to kill or cause bodily harm to agents". Witnesses disputed that she had been attempting to attack officers.

Her death sparked nationwide protests that intensified after another Minneapolis resident, Alex Pretti, was killed by immigration agents on 24 January.

Weeks later, hundreds of federal agents were withdrawn from the city and the official in charge of the operation, Greg Bovino, was removed from his post.

Granger, Good's brother, said at Thursday's news conference that "since her death no meaningful change has occurred".

"Our family is waiting and we will wait no longer," he said.

At least 10 people have been killed in encounters with immigration officers during Trump's second term, which began in January 2025, according to the Associated Press.

On Tuesday, Good's mother testified at a congressional hearing, saying: "I am a registered Republican. I voted for President Trump under the impression that these agents were here to protect the citizens of the United States.

"But far more than being a Republican, I am a Christian," she continued. "Jesus teaches us to forgive and I have, but what we are asking for is accountability."

title: Burnham criticised over support for Manchester City owners
content:
Lucy Fisher in London

Published October 1 2026

Updated October 1 2026

Downing Street has sought to downplay Andy Burnham’s backing for the owners of Manchester City, after the Conservatives accused the prime minister of politicising the Premier League’s investigation into the club.

Burnham said on Wednesday that he would be “really concerned to lose” the club’s owners, whose roles have been thrust into doubt after it was found guilty of more than 100 breaches of financial rules.

He praised the City Football Group, which is controlled by UAE vice-president Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed al-Nahyan, for having been “such a huge partner in the building of modern Manchester” during his time as mayor of the city region.

The Conservatives said the government “must keep politics out of football”, and accused the prime minister of being “out of touch” with football fans who were “horrified” by the allegations against City.

Downing Street issued a statement on Thursday clarifying that “the initial judgment is serious and there can’t be any suggestion that anyone is above the rules”.

Pointing out that Burnham had “stressed that it is an ongoing independent process”, a Number 10 spokesperson said: “If wrongdoing is established, those responsible should face the appropriate consequences.”

City have vowed to appeal against the Premier League panel’s findings, including that it artificially inflated its revenues by more than £900mn over nine years.

The episode has fuelled questions about whether the league’s enforcement of its financial rules could damage a crucial UK economic and diplomatic relationship.

Quizzed about the dilemma, Burnham acknowledged the matter could also affect both the Premier League and “brand UK”, adding that it needed to be handled “carefully without everybody jumping in and providing their conclusions”.

Recalling the dispute in which Everton, whom he supports, were found to have breached the Premier League’s financial rules in 2023, he insisted his club “weren’t treated fairly”.

He told ITV he had been “really dissatisfied with the nature of the process that had been conducted when Everton was finding itself part of an independent commission”.

Ahead of the Tory annual conference in Birmingham starting on Sunday, party leader Kemi Badenoch predicted that Burnham “is going to call an election sooner than he is saying” and speculated a poll could be called as early as next May.

Reflecting on his plans to launch a national care service, reform Britain’s electoral system, and revisit the UK’s relationship with the EU, Badenoch told BBC South East: “All the policies he announced are for after an election, so if he’s not calling an election why is he talking about things happening in 2030?”

title: Fires break out at French schools as students protest nationwide
content:
Fires have broken out at several schools in France, as students protest by blockading education institutions nationwide over school funding and studying conditions.

Blazes were reported at two high schools in Nantes, western France, while another was filmed engulfing the entrance of a school in the northern city of Rouen.

Students are protesting about a lack of teachers and staff, overcrowded classrooms and run-down buildings. University students joined the demonstrations on Thursday, citing similar demands.

The interior ministry said 1,949 people had been arrested on Thursday, with 305 police officers injured. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu held a crisis meeting on Thursday to discuss the unrest.

The government said afterwards that the student-led demonstrations had descended into "urban violence".

Both fires in Nantes spread after a bin was set alight. The blaze at the Nelson Mandela high school, in the city centre, then spread to the front of the building, damaging the entrance hall.

In the southern city of Marseille, staff at Victor Hugo high school were splashed with petrol as protesters reportedly filled containers.

While in the north, a headteacher at Degrugillier high school, in the village of Auchel, was injured in the ear by a wayward firework.

The blockades and protests at French lycées - for 15-18 year olds and equivalent to sixth forms in the UK or high schools in the US - began last week before spreading to hundreds of schools across the country.

So far, 1,027 lycees have been affected by demonstrations, with blockades at 222 of them, according to the interior ministry.

At least 30 universities have also reportedly been blockaded, including campuses in Rennes and Paris.

On Thursday, public transport services in Marseille and Strasbourg were halted due vandalism, threats of violence and to hinder protesters from moving around.

Seventeen-year-old Raphael took part in protests outside a school in Strasbourg, where barriers were used to obstruct nearby tram tracks.

He voiced his frustration at his school's facilities in an interview with news agency AFP, saying some rooms had leaks and that there were not enough toilets.

"The building is falling apart, the cafeteria is too small. There's zero budget, zero resources, not enough supervisors," Raphael said.

While France's next general election is still months away, the protests and how French authorities are responding to them has been heavily politicised.

The government and hard-right politicians have blamed the hard left for igniting protests, which are being organised by a union representing lycée students.

Bally Bagayoko, the mayor of a Parisian suburb and member of the radical left La France Insoumise (LFI) party defended earlier remarks in which he said violence could be legitimate in some cases - referencing cases in which protesters had allegedly been shot at while not wearing helmets or bulletproof vests.

LFI leader and presidential candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon, meanwhile, stressed he was in favour of non-violent protests, while arguing that blaming the left would not solve the issues motivating the demonstrations.

Earlier, leader of the hard-right National Rally Marine Le Pen said: "This is no longer about high school student protests. It is about riots organized by professionals and overseen by deputies from La France Insoumise."

The presidential candidate called for a new anti-rioting law to be passed.

Left-wing mayor of Marseille Benoît Payan condemned the "unacceptable violence" in his city.

While young people were "legitimately concerned" about their future and public services, they must express themselves in a calm fashion, he said.

Eric Ciotti, the Republicans mayor of Nice, said the parents of those found to have damaged school property should be made to pay for the repairs.

title: Algeria introduces death penalty for arsonists after deadly wildfires
content:
Algeria has adopted a law imposing the death penalty on people convicted of arson of forests or fields after a series of deadly wildfires swept parts of the country.

Members of the national assembly voted through the bill, which also made child abduction a capital offence, on Thursday.

Capital punishment has been in the country's penal code for some offences, but no execution has been carried out since 1993.

The official death toll from the blazes stands at 12, but independent news outlets believe the figure to be much higher.

Algerian President Abdelmadjid Tebboune ordered the justice ministry to introduce the changes to the criminal law after more than 100 fires in the north-east of the country during an intense heatwave in northern Africa.

Under the law, anyone convicted of deliberately setting fire to forests, woods or fields could face execution.

The death penalty has also been extended to child kidnappings that involve torture, sexual assault or mutilation.

According to news agency AFP, Justice Minister Lotfi Boudjemaa told parliament: "The adoption of the death penalty for these acts is the appropriate legal response to curb these crimes."

The tougher penalties were justified because arson had reached "the level of organised crime", with investigations suggesting links to "foreign parties", Boudjemaa said.

The upper house, the Council of the Nation, will review the law before it is officially ratified by the president.

Investigative journalist Nozha Khelalef has been gathering the names of those believed to have died in the fires from death notices posted by families and information shared by some local authorities.

Her tally, listed on the independent news website Twala, external, puts the death toll at 200.

While Algeria regularly experiences forest fires in the summer, climate change has exacerbated the intensity and severity of recent wildfires in the country.

title: Train driver accelerated through red signal before fatal crash
content:
Robert Wright in London

Published October 1 2026

Updated October 1 2026

The driver of a train involved in a fatal rail crash in Bedfordshire received an automated warning that he was passing a red signal but still accelerated before hitting another train stopped on the track, an interim report has revealed.

However, the report by the Rail Accident Investigation Branch, published on Thursday, also found the signal, near Elstow, issued a false danger warning to the Nottingham to London train that was hit in the collision on 19 June, which caused it to halt.

Following the crash, the signal had issued a second false danger alert to another train on 9 July, the report said.

The crash killed Shaun Burton, the driver of the Corby to London train that passed the red signal, and injured more than 160 people. The incident, on the Sheffield to London Midland main line, was the first fatal collision on the UK’s railways since October 2024.

The revelation that the antiquated automatic warning system (AWS) failed to prevent the crash is likely to lead to renewed calls for increased use of the train protection and warning system (TPWS), which automatically applies the brakes of any train passing a signal at danger.

TPWS was widely fitted at junctions, terminus stations and other places posing a high risk of collision in the early years of the 21st century following a series of serious crashes caused when drivers failed to respond properly to AWS warnings.

However, for cost reasons, TPWS was not fitted at locations judged lower risk such as the signal that Burton’s train passed.

An initial report published days after the crash found that Burton’s train — which investigators identified by the code 1H46 — had passed a red signal that should have protected the stationary Nottingham to London train on the track ahead. But investigators had not yet established whether Burton had correctly received an AWS warning.

Thursday’s report used information from the on-train data recorder (OTDR) — or “black box” — of the Corby to London train.

AWS issues drivers a warning if they pass signals showing red or yellow lights, but they only apply the brakes if the driver fails to acknowledge the warning within 2.7 seconds.

The report said: “The OTDR from train 1H46 recorded that the driver acknowledged the AWS warning indication, but the train continued to accelerate towards and beyond the signal, which it passed at 17:12:53.”

Burton applied the emergency brakes about 10 seconds before the impact but succeeded only in slowing the train from 75mph to 50mph.

The Nottingham to London train, meanwhile, had been forced to stop after its driver failed to respond within the required 2.7 seconds to a false AWS danger warning from the signal that Burton’s train subsequently passed at danger.

Further investigations were needed to establish why Burton did not respond correctly to the AWS danger warning before the crash, the report said.

The Department for Transport said it would ensure the rail industry acted on any findings in the RAIB’s full report when it was published.

It added: “The interim report makes clear there is still much to be established about the incident and we urge people to refrain from speculation until the full facts are set out.”

This story has been updated to correct details of AWS danger warnings

title: Christa Pike in critical condition after surviving two lethal injections, lawyer says
content:
Tennessee death row inmate Christa Pike is in "critical condition, receiving life-saving care" at hospital, after surviving two lethal injection attempts, leading the state's governor to halt all executions for the year.

"We don't have a sense of her prognosis or much update on her health at the moment," her lawyer Randy Spivey told reporters on Thursday. "But we do know that she is alive right now."

Her lawyers are now asking for her sentence to be commuted. Pike, 50, was sentenced to death in 1996 for the murder of Colleen Slemmer.

She was injected with two lethal doses of pentobarbital on Wednesday but remained alive, her lawyers said. She was then sent to hospital in an ambulance.

Pike was 18 when she and her then-boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, beat, tortured and killed 19-year-old Slemmer.

Her attempted execution on Wednesday was the subject of a last-minute legal battle. This culminated in the US Supreme Court allowing the lethal injections to go ahead.

Slemmer's mother May Martinez, who was among those who wanted the execution to take place and who travelled to Tennessee to witness it, told NBC News after the botched attempt that "it was a mess".

On Thursday afternoon, Pike's lawyers offered more details about what happened during the attempted execution, describing a harrowing scene shrouded in secrecy.

"Last night, the execution team attempted to establish an IV line for an hour," Spivey said. "I counted at least seven needles used in her left arm alone, one of which appeared to be bent when it was pulled from her arm after an unsuccessful attempt."

Spivey said that observers were kept in a dark room behind a closed curtain, after the second lethal dose had been administered and "it was clear that Miss Pike was still breathing" minutes later.

"No-one knew what was going on behind that curtain," Spivey said. "I had no idea when and if medical professionals began to assist."

Spivey said the state's governor must commute Christa's sentence now, a request that was denied previously.

Stephen Ferrell, another of Pike's lawyers, said they were also looking at other legal options.

"We want to think this through and we want to make sure that Christa recovers and has some input in what she wants," he said.

Tennessee Governor Bill Lee has ordered an independent review and said on Thursday the investigation into Pike's botched execution "will be thorough", adding that "it's going to take time".

"There are a lot of questions," Lee said. "The people of our state deserve to have those questions answered, and that's what this investigation is for."

Lee has not made clear who will conduct the independent review of the state's execution procedures.

His order to pause all executions will overlap with the planned 3 December execution of convicted murderer Gary Sutton.

The Tennessee Department of Correction, which handled the execution, issued a statement defending its handling of the case.

It said in a statement that it "followed every step of the State's lawful, established execution protocol approved by the attorney general's office".

"The lethal injection chemical in the protocol has consistently been effective, and the protocol does not allow for additional procedures beyond what was carried out this evening."

Pike was given two doses of the chemical pentobarbital, in accordance with state protocol when the first attempt fails, but was still alive afterwards, according to court filings by her lawyers.

The execution was causing Pike "unnecessary agony" and was violating her right to be executed "free of cruel and unusual punishment", her lawyers said.

The Tennessee attorney general's office said in a statement that it agreed with the decision to call for an investigation, adding: "We need to know what happened."

US Republican Senator Marsha Blackburn, who is running for Tennessee governor, described the situation as "tragic".

"While there should be a thorough review of what happened and why the process failed, the answer is simple: bring back the electric chair," Blackburn said.

Democrat Jerri Green, Blackburn's opponent, criticised her for wanting to "bring back one of the most cruel forms of capital punishment".

"As governor, I would put a moratorium on all future executions," Green said on X.

This is the second time in 2026 Tennessee officials attempted and failed to execute a prisoner.

In May, the execution of Tony Carruthers was called off after staff were unable to find a vein to administer a lethal drug. Carruthers was given a year's reprieve.

With additional reporting by Stephanie Hegarty, World Service correspondent

title: Netanyahu says Flydubai attacker had 'Islamist radical indoctrination'
content:
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu says investigations suggest the man who stabbed his fellow pilot and tried to take over a flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv had undergone "Islamist radical indoctrination".

The Flydubai plane plunged more than 17,000ft (5,200m) two hours into its journey on Wednesday, before passengers and crew overpowered the attacker and retook control to land safely.

Netanyahu told Fox News that it was looking "very likely" that the attacker, who he said was an Omani national, "was going to down the plane".

Meanwhile, the United Arab Emirates (UAE) state news agency reports investigations have begun there to determine "whether the incident was linked to any terrorist activity or purpose".

The Interior Ministry of Saudi Arabia - where the plane made an emergency landing - said that both the pilot and co-pilot had been sent back to the UAE on Thursday morning after medical teams had cleared them.

UAE officials earlier claimed jurisdiction over the incident because the aircraft on which the attack took place is registered there and flies under its flag.

Netanyahu told Fox that once the attacker had been subdued and tied up by passengers and crew, he was "calling out to the aircrew 'kill me, kill me', so it's clear he was suicidal - that's not a question".

"And with all the passengers in there, and if you couple that with what I just told you about the Islamist tendencies, that radicalisation that were found in his background, I think... that'll give us a pretty good clue."

However, he stressed that he did not want to draw any firm conclusions as to motive yet.

Both US President Donald Trump and UAE officials have indicated to the media that Iran may be responsible for the incident, without definitively blaming Tehran.

Trump told reporters on Thursday that Iran would be "hit very hard" if it was deemed to have been involved in the attack.

Pilots from countries without diplomatic relations with Israel were usually not allowed to fly there, Netanyahu said when asked about how the suspected Omani pilot came to be on the plane.

He added: "Obviously there was a loophole here and we're taking care of that among other things... with the full co-operation, I have to say, of the Emirati government, so we're both interested in making sure this doesn't happen again."

Oman has not formally established official ties with Israel, unlike the UAE.

The prime minister was also asked earlier on the same network whether there was an indication if Iran was involved, he replied: "It's too early to say".

Both Netanyahu and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi said the stabbed pilot, Indian national Capt Smit Machchhar was a "hero".

India's ambassador to the UAE Deepak Mittal visited Captain Machhar in hospital on Thursday, the Indian Mission confirmed on social media, stating he was "in good health and recovering well".

Preliminary findings from a separate Israeli investigation into the incident, suggest that the alleged attacker intended to crash the plane, an Israeli security source told BBC Arabic.

The source said the investigation - led by Israel's intelligence agency Mossad - interviewed passengers after they arrived in Tel Aviv to establish what had happened on the plane.

Flydubai's flight FZ1073, with more than 170 people on board, took off from Dubai International Airport in the UAE at 03:05 GMT (07:05 local time), en route to Ben Gurion Airport.

Two hours later, the 17,000ft drop in altitude was reported on the plane tracking website Flightradar24 and minutes later the plane signalled an emergency code.

At about 05:40, the plane - which had briefly entered Jordanian airspace - looped back into Saudi Arabia, where it later started its manual descent, landing safely at Tabuk Airport in the north west of Saudi.

Flydubai has since suspended flights between Dubai and Tel Aviv as it carried out its own investigation into the incident.

Israel's Transportation Ministry said the suspension aligns with Netanyahu's directive.

Israeli airlines including El Al, Israir and Arkia said plans were in place to operate rescue flights from Dubai starting on Friday to bring back stranded passengers.

The Transportation Ministry also said it sent an urgent request to Etihad Airlines to increase the number of flights between Abu Dhabi and Tel Aviv.

title: HMRC urged to scrutinise tax implications of Man City case
content:
Findings from the Premier League's case against Manchester City require scrutiny from His Majesty's Revenue and Customs, the chair of a cross-party group of MPs has told the tax authority.

It was confirmed on Tuesday that an independent commission found City guilty of all charges relating to breaches of the Premier League's financial regulations between the 2009-10 and 2017-18 seasons.

City have repeatedly denied guilt, and have signalled an intent to lodge an appeal by Friday.

The club were found to have artificially inflated revenue through "sham" sponsorship agreements with the help of their owners.

The independent commission which studied the case found City "utilised devices" to "disguise the true extent of certain club liabilities".

The Treasury Committee, which is responsible for overseeing policies and administration of HMRC, has therefore asked whether the government department has requested the redacted documents contained within the commission's report.

Dame Meg Hillier, chair of the Treasury Committee, said she would "welcome reassurance from HMRC that you are seized of the importance of these issues and the public interest in this case".

The letter follows a report from the Tax Policy Associates, external which claims City failed to pay as much as £12m in unpaid tax because of a "sham" contract with former manager Roberto Mancini.

In addition to unpaid income tax and National Insurance, the report claims City could face a penalty charge that would take their liabilities to £24m.

City to argue sponsorship deals came from Abu Dhabi government

Manchester City will claim as part of their appeal that key sponsorship deals were funded by the Abu Dhabi government, rather than the club's owners.

Owners Abu Dhabi United Group (ADUG) - a private investment company belonging to United Arab Emirates vice-president and deputy prime minister Sheikh Mansour - are said to have topped up the value of commercial deals as part of a "disguised funding scheme" to the scale of £830.69m.

This, it was argued, enabled the club to appear to comply with Premier League and Uefa financial rules.

However, as first reported by the Daily Mail and Times, sources have told BBC Sport that City are expected to tell an appeal board that they have evidence showing the money directed to state-owned sponsors came from the Abu Dhabi government, rather than from ADUG.

Premier League rules allow state-owned bodies to sponsor clubs.

In its 40-page decision, the independent commission detailed how City had "denied there had ever been any disguised funding scheme of the type alleged by the Premier League. Its case was that [it] had misunderstood how Abu Dhabi sponsorship agreements had been funded... The reality was [the club contested] that Abu Dhabi sponsors had always been liable for all recorded sponsorship fees and all had in fact been paid to the club by Abu Dhabi sponsors from their own funds/resources.

"No part of any recorded sponsorship fee had been paid by ADUG or from using ADUG funds. Abu Dhabi sponsors had from time to time applied for financial assistance from the Abu Dhabi government toward their liability to pay the recorded sponsorship fees - such applications had been granted…"

The independent commission rejected this submission as "untrue", saying: "We concluded that it was an 'explanation' that the club had concocted well after the event in an attempt to obscure and conceal the realities of the disguised funding scheme."

City's argument is likely to lead to renewed debate over the extent to which City's ownership is separate from the Abu Dhabi state, and over the ramifications of club ownership with state connections.

Mansour is a member of the ruling family of Abu Dhabi, and the brother of UAE President Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan.

Since the takeover in 2008, City have insisted the club is a completely private enterprise, and not state-owned. However, some critics have questioned the distinction, with human rights campaigners claiming the ownership of City has been used to "sportswash" the UAE.

On Saturday, City chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak referred to "irrefutable evidence" that he claimed supports the club's claims of innocence. City have claimed the commission's decision contained "clear material errors, of law, principle and fact, and is unsafe".

It has emerged that Al Mubarak, who was appointed chairman of City following the takeover in 2008, is named as an Emirati diplomat on the UK government's current directory of all foreign representatives.

Representatives of foreign states and their diplomatic staff "enjoy privileges and immunities under the Diplomatic Privileges Act (1964)", giving diplomats immunity from prosecution under criminal, civil and administrative laws.

City's principal sponsor Etihad Airways has said it is considering legal action against the Premier League, claiming the release of the commission findings had "damaging implications… despite the airline not being named in the redacted published findings".

The UAE's state-owned national airline said it "categorically rejects any finding, conclusion or implication that suggests the airline has ever been involved in improper commercial arrangements".

Etihad is owned by sovereign wealth fund L'Imad which is chaired by the Crown Prince of Abu Dhabi, the son of the UAE president.

The Premier League declined to comment when contacted by BBC Sport.

Additional reporting from James Landale, diplomatic correspondent for BBC News.

title: Prince of Wales tells villagers 'holistic' approach is needed to tackle flooding
content:
The Prince of Wales has said a "holistic" approach is needed to tackle severe flooding, as a small Welsh village prepares for the upcoming storm season.

Residents in Skenfrith, Monmouthshire, have faced four major floods in the past six years.

An extreme flood last winter had a devastating impact on the village, when the River Monnow burst its banks after Storm Claudia brought a month's worth of rain in just 24 hours to parts of England and Wales.

Prince William was visiting the area to learn about how communities have been affected by recent flooding and what measures were being taken by local authorities and other agencies to mitigate future incidents.

Over the years, families have reported that their homes and possessions had been destroyed by the floods. In 2019, about 25 homes were evacuated in the village following flooding and a power cut after heavy rain.

The prince sympathised with residents who might be "anxious" about extreme weather events he said were no longer "one in 50-year" occurrences but instead seemed to be happening every year.

On Thursday, the prince spoke to villagers Rod and Helen Wyatt at their garden gate and was told how the water almost topped gravestones in a cemetery opposite during a flood.

The couple have now tiled the ground floor of their house and live with the threat of further flooding.

Rod, who has lived in his home for 10 years, made light of the experience when he told Prince William that, at one point, "we had to give up really, we got two bottles of Prosecco and went to watch Strictly upstairs".

The prince replied: "It must be so demoralising for you now, the worry each year you've got to go through that again, potentially, is becoming more frequent.

"They keep talking about a one in 50-year event, it doesn't make sense anymore.

"It might be in the researching and scientific point of view - it's happening every year now, it's mad.

"So, it's trying to understand how we can do a better holistic view of the whole catchment area, so we're dealing with the whole problem."

He listed a number of ideas, from "slowing the water down" using farming landscaping remedies, to tree planting and better monitoring "so we know when things might be getting worse".

Prince William discussed the ideas in detail while later meeting representatives from environmental charity Stump Up for Trees at Great Tre-Rhew Farm in Monmouthshire.

The charity, founded in 2020, aims to plant one million native trees across south Wales and Bannau Brycheiniog, also known as the Brecon Beacons.

The prince joined volunteers harvesting seeds from a field maple tree and planted a sessile oak tree - designated as the national tree of Wales.

To access the trees, he had to climb over a barbed wire fence and use a small step, joking that he did not want to rip his trousers.

As he harvested seeds from the tree, he noted he was taller than others present, adding: "I'm going to reach up here and get these higher ones."

The charity collected 35,000 seeds last year that were used to grow new trees for planting, and hopes to increase this to 60,000 this year.

The prince spoke to Kate and Jim Beavan, of Great Tre-Rhew Farm, and Jenny Knight, the director of Stump Up for Trees.

After the visit, Knight paid tribute to Prince William for "looking at not just the problems but the solutions as well".

Representatives from the Duchy of Cornwall also joined the visit to share learning about nature recovery, climate-resilient forestry and to start a long-term partnership.

Knight added "knowledge exchange is so valuable" and said working together across different areas would have a greater impact.

At the end of the conversation, William discussed his enjoyment of cider, which is made on the farm.

"He said 'one pint a day keeps the doctor away'," Knight said.

Prince William also visited Herefordshire and met farmer Harry Davies, 25, who is set to lead the Duchy of Cornwall's first regenerative farming project on a 25-year lease at the 900-acre farm.

The project aims to improve soil health and make farms more resilient to flooding and drought.

Davies said: "By us being able to hold that water in that soil profile so it doesn't go into our rivers and streams quite so quickly, we should be able to hold the water on our land. Which in the long term will then benefit us when it's hot and dry.

"There seems to be an opportunity to draw on experience from my Grandad's generation, but also a bit of youth and enthusiasm is also needed. I think it's about generations working together, that's just farming."

title: Lib Dem MPs criticise Davey over pension triple lock response
content:
Liberal Democrat MPs have criticised their party leader over his defence of the pension triple lock.

Senior Lib Dems, who are on the party's frontbench, have privately attacked Sir Ed Davey for his response to the prime minister's plans to adjust the policy, which guarantees the state pension goes up each year in line with either inflation, wage increases, or 2.5% – whichever is highest.

They joined unsolicited criticism in public and private from others in the party, with one saying the majority of Lib Dem MPs disagree with their leader.

It comes after Sir Ed told the BBC removing the triple lock "would put more pensioners into poverty".

"This would mean people who are working hard now - the millennials - when they retire would have a very poor pension," he told the Today programme.

Under Andy Burnham's plan - which he hopes will raise £15bn a year by the end of the 2030s - the automatic annual link with average earnings would be removed from 2030 so the state pension rises with at least 2.5% or inflation, whichever is higher.

"His proposals are to deal with social care in the next decade when it needs to be done now," Sir Ed said.

"It's a little bit of a vibe. It's not a solution," he said.

But multiple Lib Dems at different levels have now criticised Sir Ed's response.

A Lib Dem MP contacted the BBC after Sir Ed's interview to say the majority of the parliamentary party would not support opposing Burnham's changes to the triple lock.

Another, Tom Gordon, who represents Harrogate & Knaresborough, said Sir Ed's criticism of Burnham's plan to adjust the triple lock was "nonsense" and "gaslights an entire generation into believing it's for our benefit".

He wrote on X: "The idea that we're keeping the triple lock to help millennials is at best for the birds, and at worst downright insulting. I say that as a millennial."

He added: "Telling millennials we're keeping the triple lock to help us in 30 years' time is nonsense.

"We're on course to be the first generation worse off than our parents. We're locked out of the housing market, paying higher taxes, repaying student loans that never seem to shrink, and putting off having children because of the cost of living."

Vikki Slade, the party's MP for Mid-Dorset and North Poole, said on Bluesky: "Most millennials don't think there will be a state pension when they retire so this isn't being done with them in mind."

She added that she was "proud" of the triple lock when it was introduced by the Conservative-Liberal Democrat coalition government in 2010, "but we must plan for future not venerate the past".

A Lib Dem spokesperson said: "The triple lock has always been controversial.

"It's done a lot of good but its job isn't done yet, so Labour's plan would push too many of today's workers into poverty when they retire.

"We want Andy Burnham to get back around the table so that we can find a lasting consensus on social care with a sustainable funding model - not one pulled out of the pockets of a group of people who can least afford it."

The Lib Dems, and other opposition parties, are battling to respond to a new set of priorities from the Labour government under Burnham.

One frontbench Lib Dem MP told the BBC after Burnham's Labour conference speech: "Lots of us [are] struggling tonight with [a] Labour leader articulating Lib Dem values better than we do."

They pointed to Burnham's promises on electoral reform, social care, the water industry, and relations with Europe - all Lib Dem campaign points in recent years.

"I'm honestly utterly despondent with the state of things," another Lib Dem MP said.

Some senior Lib Dems believe Sir Ed's position as leader has been vulnerable for some time, even if they stressed no challenge is imminent.

"A plausible candidate could take him tomorrow in a bloodless coup," one prominent party figure said.

"But that person hasn't yet revealed themselves as far as I'm aware. Nobody is going to blow anything up without a clear plan to put something in its place."

title: Man City not 'above the rules', says No 10 after backlash to Burnham remarks
content:
Downing Street has said Manchester City are not "above the rules" after Andy Burnham was criticised for his comments about the club's breaches of Premier League financial rules.

The prime minister said on Wednesday he would be "really concerned" if the club's owners decided to sell up after City were found guilty by an independent commission of most of the 115 charges they faced.

His remarks were branded "completely out of touch" and "extraordinary" by the Tories and took many in the football community by surprise.

In a statement following the backlash, Downing Street said the PM had made clear "the initial judgement is serious and there can't be any suggestion that anyone is above the rules".

In an attempt to clarify the PM's position, a No 10 spokesperson added: "He also stressed that it is an ongoing independent process. It is essential that it is allowed to run its course and the outcome respected.

"Wherever wrongdoing is established, those responsible should face the appropriate consequences."

Man City deny any wrongdoing and have until Friday to submit an appeal.

Sources told BBC Sport that City were expected to claim that key sponsorship deals were funded by the Abu Dhabi government, rather than the club's owners, as part of an appeal.

Among the independent panel's findings were that City arranged "sham contracts" with a number of commercial partners as part of a scheme to disguise secret funding of more than £830m.

The Premier League says City "systematically broke Premier League Rules for nearly a decade".

In an interview on Wednesday with the BBC's political editor Chris Mason, Burnham - who was mayor of Greater Manchester until June - said he was "not getting directly involved in the process" and that it must be undertaken independently by the Premier League.

He said the situation was "contested by Manchester City" and it would be "wrong" to "jump to a conclusion".

Asked if he was worried the club's owners since 2008 - led by Sheikh Mansour, a royal and the United Arab Emirates deputy prime minister - might sell up, Burnham replied: "I would be really concerned to lose them.

"They've been such a huge partner in the building of modern Manchester and obviously the building of Manchester City into the global force that it is.

"I can't intervene more in the process, it would be wrong for me to do that."

The Tories have accused Burnham of "publicly backing the owners even as the investigation continues" and questioned whether "political pressure" was being applied.

Shadow minister for sport Louie French called for the government to "keep politics out of football and ensure the Premier League's independent commission can do its job free of outside influence".

"The club face unprecedented allegations and fans are horrified by what they are reading in the papers," the Tory MP said.

"Yet Burnham is publicly backing the owners even as the investigation continues. Fans will rightly ask whether political pressure is being applied here and how it relates to the owners' well-reported investments in Manchester.

"Football must be governed independently, with the rules applying equally to everyone. Fans deserve confidence that no club or owner is above those rules."

And Lib Dem MP Anna Sabine, the party's spokesperson on sport, said: "Fans of every club deserve to know the rules apply to everyone... Burnham needs to remember he's prime minister for everyone, not just Manchester."

The chairwoman of the Commons Treasury committee, Labour MP Dame Meg Hillier, wrote to HMRC on Thursday to ask for reassurance that it had "seized of the importance" of the case for any potential tax implications.

In his BBC interview, Burnham also said he was "of course" confident that his own interactions with City's owners as Greater Manchester mayor would stand up to scrutiny.

He compared City's situation to how the club he supports, Everton, had been charged with a more minor breach of Premier League financial rules in 2023, but said he "hold[s] the view very firmly that they weren't fairly treated in that process".

Burnham made his comments amid widespread shock in football about the scale of the independent commission's findings – and the strength of Premier League comments about City's actions.

The independent panel that found City guilty of rule breaches will hold a sanctions hearing – which could take months to convene – to decide the punishment, which could include a huge fine or points deduction.

City have maintained their innocence of all the accusations made.

The chairman of the Independent Football Regulator (IFR) – set up by the government in 2025 – said the case had raised "serious issues".

In a statement, David Kogan said the IFR "has powers to assess the suitability of owners, directors and executives and we will use these powers where appropriate", while "taking account of the findings made by the Leagues".

He added that proceedings remain ongoing and he hoped for a quick resolution.

A former chairman of Man City and the Football Association told the BBC's Newsnight programme he was "concerned" by Burnham's comments on the club's breaches.

David Bernstein, who chaired City from 1998 to 2003, said: "It is absolutely vital that this independent regulator can perform independently and without political interference."

Asked if he had any advice for Burnham, he said: "I would suggest he's got other fish to fry and this is something that politicians should be seen to be staying well away from."

title: EU countries in crisis talks over release of diesel stocks
content:
Ian Johnston and Henry Foy in Brussels and Anne-Sylvaine Chassany in Berlin

Published October 1 2026

Updated October 1 2026

Could you be the FT’s top trader?

European countries are in crisis talks over the release of diesel stocks, as the US threatens them with a diesel export ban unless they release strategic reserves of the oil product.

Three people familiar with the matter said the US administration had put pressure on European countries to release strategic stocks of diesel, warning that it could ban US diesel exports if they do not do so.

The EU’s energy commissioner Dan Jørgensen had held talks with officials from France, Germany, the UK, Italy and Ireland on Thursday, in an attempt to co-ordinate and develop a joint response to the threats from Donald Trump, an official said. No decision was taken on a release, they added.

“We are in very close contact to co-ordinate with our member states how we go forward and we have on a separate track also high-level contacts with the US administration on this,” said Anna-Kaisa Itkonen, a spokesperson for the European Commission. These were “intense contacts given the ongoing situation”, she added.

A Trump administration official told the FT: “It is in Europe’s best interests to work with the United States as we pursue multiple pathways to boost the supply of refined products and lower costs for consumers.”

Trump is under intense pressure to lower prices at the pump ahead of US midterm elections. The US oil industry has urged the president’s administration to ask European allies to release diesel stocks as part of a frenetic lobbying campaign in Washington this week aiming to prevent a US export ban.

One person in the industry told the FT that Europe may hold up to 400mn barrels of diesel in commercial inventories and stockpiles, which, if released, could bring down global prices.

The oil industry has told the Trump administration that a diesel ban would undermine its efforts to promote the US as a reliable energy exporter and could backfire by pushing up prices of petrol and other products.

Donald Trump says he is still considering if to bring in a diesel export ban

Members of the International Energy Agency in March agreed to release 400mn barrels of emergency stocks globally to calm oil markets. At that time, Europe said it would release 32.7mn barrels of government stocks and 74.8mn barrels of industry reserves, 70 per cent of which were oil products. The Americas provided 172mn barrels, with the US releasing the remainder of its stocks on Tuesday.

Announcing the release, US energy secretary Chris Wright said: “While the United States and Japan are delivering on their commitments, several European member countries have released only a fraction of the crude oil and petroleum products they pledged. We urge every member country to fulfil its commitments.”

Fatih Birol, head of the IEA, said on Tuesday that some European countries had not yet released all the stocks they had committed to in March. “The countries have already made major efforts in Europe. A big chunk of the stocks have been released, but still some remain, both in terms of crude oil and products,” he told journalists.

Earlier on Thursday, Reuters reported that the US administration wanted the EU to release 120mn barrels over six months.

“The US is pressuring Europe to release more of their reserves which are heavily weighted towards diesel, with 195mn barrels on paper,” said analysts at consultancy Energy Aspects.

“However, we believe governments are unlikely to release all pledged volumes too hastily or at once, given the uncertainty surrounding the ongoing conflicts in the Middle East and between Russia and Ukraine. They know releasing the [strategic reserves] will be the last bullet in the chamber.”

Bob McNally, founder of energy analysis group Rapidan and a former adviser to George W Bush, said: “European countries have not complied with their pledged strategic stock releases, which include diesel fuel. If Europe steps up on pledged diesel stock draws, the US may step back on restricting exports.”

A German official said the country had received “no new requests from the IEA” to release reserves. “As a general rule, the market must not be destabilised,” the official cautioned.

Additional reporting by Jamie Smyth in Washington and Malcolm Moore in London

title: BT seeks government nod for potential TalkTalk takeover
content:
Kieran Smith in Brussels

Published October 1 2026

BT has opened talks with UK government officials over the possibility of a takeover bid for struggling rival TalkTalk, as the country’s largest broadband provider prepares a late entrance into the auction for the heavily indebted company.

Allison Kirkby, chief executive of the FTSE 100 telecoms group, this week met officials at the Department for Culture, Media and Sport to seek assurances that a takeover of TalkTalk would not trigger an in-depth antitrust review, according to three people familiar with the matter.

BT is interested in buying the company’s wholesale and retail businesses, two of the people said.

Its broadband network Openreach, which is deemed by industry watchdog Ofcom to have significant market power, is TalkTalk’s largest supplier. The division covers more than 30mn UK homes, almost 25mn of them with full fibre.

People familiar with the TalkTalk auction said that it had been held up partly by other bidders’ concerns over the quantum of fees payable to Openreach.

Meanwhile, BT is also the country’s largest broadband provider with 30 per cent market share, according to estimates from Enders Analysis.

BT is working with antitrust lawyers at Clifford Chance on the possible TalkTalk deal, some of the people said.

TalkTalk’s owners, which include founder Sir Charles Dunstone and private capital group Ares, have been seeking a buyer for the troubled business for months. The company was previously in exclusive negotiations to offload its wholesale business to Octopus Investments and its consumer operations, which serve 1.6mn customers, to Opus Broadband.

However, neither party has been able to reach an agreement, forcing TalkTalk to explore options including a break-up that would potentially carve up the company between private capital group Epiris and Ares, its largest creditor. Talks with several potential buyers are ongoing, according to one of the people.

The company’s existing shareholders have been forced to inject money into the business to cover shortfalls on several occasions.

BT is hoping to have gained enough clarity over the antitrust situation to be able to make a decision over a deal for TalkTalk by the weekend, one of the people said.

Karen Egan, head of telecoms at Enders Analysis, said that “when companies get to the level of distress that TalkTalk appears to be in, competition concerns tend to take a back seat.”

“In this instance, the government will be more concerned about security and continuity of service for vulnerable customers,” she added.

TalkTalk has struggled since it was taken private by Toscafund, a London-based hedge fund, in a £1.1bn leveraged buyout in 2021 that added £527mn of debt to its balance sheet. The company’s retail customer base has fallen from more than 2.5mn in 2023 to about 1.6mn in May.

Shareholders injected £235mn into TalkTalk as part of a refinancing in December 2024 and then a further £120mn in July last year. Ares pumped in another £115mn in March.

A DCMS spokesperson said that “this is a commercial matter and we do not comment on speculation”.

TalkTalk, BT, Ares and Epiris declined to comment. Clifford Chance did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Additional reporting by Jim Pickard in London

title: Dealmakers line up to test EU’s appetite to create European champions
content:
Barbara Moens

Published October 1 2026

For companies, bankers and corporate lawyers around Europe, there is a sudden scramble under way to recast how they pitch a series of big mergers and acquisitions to regulators.

The EU is signalling that it is opening the door to bigger corporate mergers, allowing European companies to gain the scale needed to compete with Chinese and American rivals.

So in response, companies and their advisers are framing their planned deals as test cases for this new approach, betting that arguments about the need for European champions, resilience and investment will help win approval.

Several potential contentious transactions in industries ranging from mining to elevators — and one including a satellite tie-up between Airbus, Thales and Leonardo — are set to provide first indications in the coming months of whether the change in language translates into a more permissive approach to consolidation.

European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen has emphasised the need for European champions and cast competition policy as an important part of the bloc’s competitiveness agenda. Meanwhile, her competition chief Teresa Ribera has been explicit in saying the new approach does not amount to a blank cheque for consolidation.

For businesses, that unusual divide over policy leaves one crucial question: how much will actually change?

“Businesses and investors need to see a body of coherent precedent showing how the framework will operate in practice, and it’s for businesses and advisers to work constructively with the commission to achieve this,” said Rafique Bachour of law firm Skadden Arps.

That body of precedent does not yet exist. So, as one Brussels-based M&A-lawyer, points out: “Every big case will now be packaged differently and presented as a test case to create a European champion.”

There is no shortage of candidates. The proposed joint venture between paper manufacturers UPM and Sappi has left the commission concerned it will restrict competition in the markets and give the companies the ability to increase prices. However, the companies argue the deal is the only way to stay competitive and maintain the security of supply in a shrinking industry grappling with excess capacity.

Anglo American’s planned sale of its Brazilian nickel assets to China-backed MMG is seen as a test of how far Brussels is willing to go in its stronger China policy. The case ticks boxes for both resilience and security of supply.

Further down the pipeline is a bid by Finnish lift maker Kone to buy its rival TK Elevator, a deal that from a traditional antitrust perspective would be seen as a steep uphill battle. Whether European competition officials will now assess it through a different lens will be closely watched by dealmakers.

But the clearest test of Brussels’ new philosophy is emerging in space. Airbus, Leonardo and Thales want to combine their satellite business in a venture designed to create a European player capable of better competing with Elon Musk’s SpaceX. Its competitors warn it would weaken competition, ultimately increasing costs for taxpayers.

The mix of traditional merger policy, industrial policy and geopolitical competition makes the joint venture, dubbed Project Bromo, “the obvious test case and a no-brainer”, another lawyer said.

In unusually public remarks about an upcoming antitrust review, von der Leyen referred to the Bromo merger in a recent speech and said “these are the types of industrial champions we need if Europe is to lead in the space economy of tomorrow”.

Ribera subsequently defended the independence of European antitrust officials, many of whom are already nervous about the new political winds. The Spanish competition commissioner made clear that von der Leyen’s comments did not mean “we are not going to apply and to enforce our own regulation”.

Some antitrust experts argued von der Leyen should have given her political steer more subtly. But for companies and deal markets, more clarity is welcome.

That is acknowledged by some European Commission officials, well aware their in-tray is being closely watched. “We need one deal that shows we are serious about the shift,” said one.
